conversation.content:
*gentle smile*  
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’ll be spending the next few minutes with you to do a quick check-in on how things have felt since your baby arrived.  

We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the first year postpartum, and it also asks about self-harm so we can keep you safe.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the medical record unless you tell me you’re in danger of hurting yourself or someone else; then we’d need to bring in extra support. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you in the past seven days.  

I’ll re-phrase each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels easiest. Ready to start?

Question 1  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty impossible?

*looks down at hands, then back up*

I... I can laugh sometimes, I guess. Like yesterday my husband made a silly joke and I smiled for a second. But mostly... nothing really feels funny anymore. It's like there's this heaviness that makes everything feel flat. I watched a show I used to love and just stared at it feeling nothing.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*nods slowly*

Yeah… that’s… that’s not me. I haven’t really been able to laugh much at all. Things that used to crack me up—like my favorite sitcom or my husband’s dumb impressions—just feel kind of pointless now. I *want* to laugh, but it’s like the switch is stuck.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, voice soft*

Mostly… no. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one big “meh.” I still do them, because I think I *should*, but that spark, that looking-forward feeling, it’s just… gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*eyes water a little*

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right, or my milk isn’t good enough. When I dropped a burp cloth on the floor yesterday I felt like the worst mom. It’s like every little hiccup turns into proof I’m failing him.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*twists the edge of my sleeve*

I’m pretty much anxious all the time, even when everything looks fine. I’ll check that he’s breathing over and over, or lie awake imagining the stroller tipping into traffic. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, we’re safe—but the thoughts just keep looping and I can’t snap out of it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*presses palms together tightly*

Yeah… a few times this week. Like yesterday, I was just feeding the baby in the rocking chair and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t breathe. Nothing happened—no loud noise, nothing—but I had to put him in the crib real quick and go splash water on my face. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky the rest of the evening.
Things have been getting on top of me

*lets out a slow breath, eyes on the floor*

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in small stuff—laundry, dishes, trying to answer one text. I’ll start one task and then the baby cries, and suddenly everything piles up and I just… freeze. I’m managing, I guess, but it’s like walking through thick mud all the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods slowly, voice low*

That’s been happening almost every night. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—mostly worries about the baby, replaying everything I might’ve done wrong. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and then I jerk awake at every little sound, heart pounding. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

*swallows hard*

Yeah… pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud parked over me—I’ll be feeding the baby or folding onesies and just feel this heavy sadness out of nowhere. Some afternoons I’ll stare out the window and cry for five minutes, then wipe my face and keep going.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, eyes glassy*

Yes… that’s me. A couple of times this week it just spilled over—like yesterday when I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded at the mailbox. I stood there in the street with tears running down my face, feeling ridiculous but unable to stop. It happens when everything feels too heavy and I can’t hold it in anymore.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*quiet for a moment, picking at a loose thread on the hospital gown*

…once or twice. Nothing planned, just these quick flashes—like when I’m rocking him at 3 a.m. and I think, “What if I just disappeared?” They’re gone as fast as they come, but they shake me up. I’d never act on them; I just want the pressure inside me to stop.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, hospital day #2 ( gown) – self-report via EPDS-style interview  

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>  
- Anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent low mood, daily crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to ruminative worry (Q7)  
- Pathologic guilt / self-blame over routine infant care (Q3)  
- Chronic free-floating anxiety + discrete panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Overwhelm / “frozen” functioning with routine tasks (Q6)  

<med>Pattern</med>: Symptoms cluster consistent with major depressive episode with anxious features, onset within first weeks postpartum.  

Risk factors  
- Daily impairment in self-care and infant care  
- Present but passive self-harm ideation (“disappear” flashes, no plan/intent) → safety flag  
- Absence of protective factors not yet assessed (support system, prior mental health treatment)  

Screening impression  
High likelihood of current postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; passive suicidal ideation present. Recommend immediate psychiatric evaluation, safety plan, and consideration of inpatient mother-baby unit transfer while medical inpatient.
